/-!
# Erdős Problem 46

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/46](https://www.erdosproblems.com/46)
- [Cr03] Croot, III, Ernest S., *On a coloring conjecture about unit fractions*. Ann. of Math. (2)
  (2003), 545-556.
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
-/

namespace Erdos46

/--
Does every finite colouring of the integers have a monochromatic solution to
$1=\sum \frac{1}{n_i}$ with $2\leq n_1<\cdots <n_k$?

The answer is yes, as proved by Croot [Cr03] - indeed, there are infinitely many disjoint such
monochromatic solutions.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 11, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos46.lean"]
theorem erdos_46 :
    answer(True) ↔
    -- For any finite colouring of the integers
    ∀ (𝓒 : ℕ → ℕ), (Set.range 𝓒).Finite →
      -- there are integers `2 ≤ n₁ < ⋯ < n_k`
      ∃ S : Finset ℕ, (∀ n ∈ S, 2 ≤ n) ∧
        -- whose reciprocals sum to `1`
        ∑ n ∈ S, (1 / n : ℚ) = 1 ∧
        -- and which all have the same colour
        (𝓒 '' (S : Set ℕ)).Subsingleton := by
  sorry

/--
Croot [Cr03] proved more: there are infinitely many disjoint such monochromatic solutions.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_46.variants.infinitely_many_disjoint :
    answer(True) ↔
    ∀ (𝓒 : ℕ → ℕ), (Set.range 𝓒).Finite →
      ∃ S : ℕ → Finset ℕ, (∀ i j, i ≠ j → Disjoint (S i) (S j)) ∧
        ∀ i, (∀ n ∈ S i, 2 ≤ n) ∧ ∑ n ∈ S i, (1 / n : ℚ) = 1 ∧
          (𝓒 '' (S i : Set ℕ)).Subsingleton := by
  sorry

/--
In [ErGr80] they also ask for a monochromatic representation of any $\frac{a}{b}>0$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_46.variants.positive_rat :
    answer(True) ↔
    ∀ (𝓒 : ℕ → ℕ), (Set.range 𝓒).Finite → ∀ q : ℚ, 0 < q →
      ∃ S : Finset ℕ, (∀ n ∈ S, 2 ≤ n) ∧ ∑ n ∈ S, (1 / n : ℚ) = q ∧
        (𝓒 '' (S : Set ℕ)).Subsingleton := by
  sorry

end Erdos46

reformulations.difference: Uses finite-range colourings ℕ → ℕ and an unordered Finset of denominators, rather than a finite colouring of the integers and a strictly increasing list 2 ≤ n₁ < ⋯ < nₖ. Monochromaticity is expressed by subsingleton image.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: A finite range can be encoded by a finite palette, and every finite palette embeds into ℕ. Integer colourings restrict to ℕ; natural-number colourings extend to ℤ using Int.toNat, without changing any permitted denominator. A Finset has distinct elements and admits a strictly increasing enumeration. Conversely, such an enumeration gives a Finset with the same reciprocal sum. The positive sum excludes the empty set, so subsingleton image means exactly one colour occurs. These reductions were combined into Review46.full_main_equivalence in the scratch file.

reformulations.difference: The family is monochromatic separately at each index, without explicitly requiring a single colour shared by the whole family, as used in the source's subsequent rational-representation argument.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Each unit-sum set is nonempty. Pairwise disjointness therefore prevents repeated sets and makes the sequence genuinely infinite. Choose the colour of each set; all these colours lie in the finite range of the colouring. Infinite pigeonhole yields an infinite subsequence of one colour, preserving disjointness and all reciprocal sums. The converse is immediate. Review46.infiniteFamily_iff_commonColor proves this equivalence; nonemptiness and injectivity were also proved independently.

reformulations.difference: Lean permits the colour to depend on q. The website likewise asks for a monochromatic representation of any positive rational, but ErGr80, p. 37, says 'one class always contains integers whose reciprocals sum to each rational a/b', admitting the stronger reading of one colour for all positive rationals.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Even the uniform-colour reading is equivalent to the globally quantified Lean principle. Lean's rational assertion gives the unit-sum assertion U by q = 1. U gives solutions avoiding any finite forbidden set: recolour its elements with separate fresh colours, whose singleton classes cannot sum to 1 with denominators ≥ 2. Iteration and infinite pigeonhole give infinitely many disjoint unit solutions in one colour. For any b ≥ 1, apply this to n ↦ C(bn). Scaling denominators gives a colour with infinitely many disjoint representations of 1/b, hence representations of every a/b by finite unions. If no colour represented all positive rationals, choose a missing positive rational q_j for each of the finitely many colours and a common denominator b. The colour obtained for this b represents its own missing q_j, a contradiction. The uniform assertion immediately implies the per-rational assertion. If denominator 1 is allowed in the book's formulation, isolate it in a fresh colour; that colour cannot represent all positive rationals.
